title: Internal drainage of a supralevator collection

cues.phrase: Ischioanal fat contains no communicating cavity; abdominal imaging shows no visceral source.
cues.why: This single row supplies two option-specific negatives beside alternatives named 'through the ischioanal space' and 'Transabdominal drainage'. A nonmedical elimination strategy can reject both routes without interpreting the positive intersphincteric anatomy.

fairness: The communicating intersphincteric origin supports internal drainage. Inferring origin and applying the drainage-plane rule are consequential steps; no confident clinical error is identified in the key or explanation.
Standalone chronology is clear. This is a high-yield surgical anatomy and source-control distinction, although the exclusion row reduces the intended challenge.

Review scope: all 22 rewritten/new executable nodes were assessed from their candidate presentation, updates, exhibits, tasks, option labels and explanations, including preceding visible feedback. Two kept records, 65 retirement proposals, and held/parked records were noted but not adjudicated. No network or source verification was performed. All verdicts are editorial, difficulty is qualitative, and none confers clinical approval.
suggestions: Keep the positive continuity observations and any genuinely necessary exclusion of an abdominal source. Rework the alternative routes so the two negatives do not individually dispose of the entire distractor set; compare credible routes for the demonstrated source plane.
Do not erase decision-critical anatomy simply to increase difficulty. Re-solve the revised set with the options covered.

title: External drainage of an ascending ischioanal collection
fairness: The resident must identify the lateral compartment from its relationship to the external sphincter, then select drainage following the infected plane. External transperineal drainage is the best of the supplied routes.

The alternatives are parallel routes. The negative abdominal finding weakens one alternative but does not by itself resolve the consequential internal-versus-external choice. No diagnosis label, unique teaching clause, convergence pattern or strong key-only wording shortcut was found.

The retrospective timing is coherent and the task is complete. This tests a high-yield source-control distinction. No confident clinical inaccuracy is identified; this remains an offline editorial assessment.
suggestions: Preserve the positive anatomical relationships and route-based option structure. Treat this and the internal-drainage sibling as complementary applications of one rule, not evidence of independent hard-level difficulty after repeated exposure.

title: Residual deep postanal source after lateral drainage
clarityIssues: Calling the posterior pocket 'separate' and then describing channels to both lateral cavities can momentarily suggest an isolated pocket. Distinguish a residual loculation from a disconnected collection.

cues.phrase: A separate fluid pocket remains behind the anal canal below the levator.
cues.why: Only one option explicitly drains this named remaining pocket; the other plans mention lateral incisions only. The uniquely comprehensive plan can be selected by coverage matching.

cues.phrase: The old incision opens a decompressed lateral cavity.
cues.why: This expressly makes enlarging that same incision a weak alternative before any horseshoe anatomy is interpreted.

fairness: Including the deep postanal source in drainage is clinically coherent and high yield. The exhibit supports the general keyed plan.

The exact need for a new left counterincision is less clear because the left opening is already patent and that cavity decompressed. The wording should allow use of an adequate existing opening rather than imply that a redundant new incision is mandatory.
The supplied choices reduce the task to draining every explicitly named undrained space. That does not sustain two consequential resident-level inferences.
suggestions: Specify the operative problem as access to the residual posterior source and compare anatomically credible approaches that all address it.
Describe how the existing left drain participates in the plan and avoid requiring an unnecessary additional incision. Clarify that the posterior cavity communicates with the lateral arms.

title: Definitive treatment of a low fistula with intact continence
fairness: The tract crosses only the lowest external sphincter fibers, is unbranched, and occurs in a previously unoperated man with intact continence. These observations support selected lay-open fistulotomy over the offered sphincter-preserving repairs.

Two consequential judgments remain: classify the extent of muscle involvement and combine it with functional reserve to choose a procedure. The description supplies neither the label 'simple fistula' nor a sphincter-preservation slogan.

All options are named definitive operations. The short keyed label is not by itself a reliable shortcut. The standalone case is coherent and the objective is high yield; no confident clinical error is identified.
suggestions: Retain the low crossing, baseline function and lack of previous fistula surgery. Do not replace these observations with an authored eligibility conclusion or an unsupported numerical muscle threshold.

title: Mapping recurrent fistula beyond a known sphincter defect

cues.phrase: Endoanal ultrasound focused on the old sphincter defect
cues.why: The qualifier deliberately restricts a potentially useful anatomical test to a previously documented finding. 'Old' versus the new openings makes the key the only broadly relevant anatomical investigation.

cues.phrase: Pelvic MRI with a dedicated fistula protocol
cues.why: Only the key is framed as a dedicated investigation of the disease being planned for; the alternatives address the old defect or physiological function. This is a scope-of-label advantage.

fairness: Recurrent branching or deep disease warrants anatomical mapping, and dedicated MRI is a defensible best answer here. The new distribution and higher induration are useful clinical observations.

The problem is the artificially restricted ultrasound alternative, not a confident error in choosing MRI. A broadly specified expert ultrasound can also contribute to fistula assessment; do not teach that it evaluates only continence defects.
The high-yield objective currently collapses to choosing the only option that investigates the new fistula anatomy. The standalone chronology is clear.
suggestions: Offer investigations with comparable scope and a real distinction in mapping the demonstrated higher extension. If MRI must outrank an adequate ultrasound, supply the decision-critical limitation neutrally rather than narrowing the distractor to the old defect.
Keep the old continence injury as a relevant constraint, but make interpreting the new anatomy change a genuine planning decision.

title: Evaluation of lateral anal lesions with inflammatory bowel symptoms

cues.phrase: combined anal and bowel findings
cues.why: The task explicitly favors the only option inspecting bowel mucosa. The other two labels concern sphincter structure or anorectal physiology, so the task itself narrows the answer category.

fairness: Multiple lateral lesions plus diarrhea, nocturnal bowel movements and weight loss reasonably support ileocolonoscopy with sampling for a secondary intestinal disorder. The explanation correctly avoids declaring a final diagnosis.

The alternatives do not plausibly investigate the stated inflammatory symptom cluster. The item tests an important recognition rule but supplies no serious competing etiologic evaluation, so two-step difficulty is not established.
The patient and standalone task are otherwise clear. No confident clinical inaccuracy is identified.
suggestions: Use a neutral next-investigation task and compare credible etiologic workups for atypical anal ulceration, with supported observations distinguishing intestinal inflammation from another plausible cause.
Retain the alarm symptoms and off-midline distribution; do not create difficulty by withholding them.

title: Topical therapy after nitrate intolerance
clarityIssues: The painful presentation and broad request for a 'medication' leave healing treatment versus symptom relief implicit. The explanation addresses healing-oriented treatment, whereas lidocaine addresses pain.

cues.phrase: He had not tried diltiazem
cues.why: The stem names the keyed medication as the conspicuous untried treatment.

cues.phrase: Each attempt at glyceryl trinitrate caused a severe headache and he stopped the ointment.
cues.why: Reoffering the same intolerable drug is an easily eliminated distractor. Combined with the named untried drug, a learner need not reason through treatment mechanism or stage.

fairness: Topical diltiazem is a reasonable alternative after nitrate intolerance. The statement about tolerability is broadly coherent; no confident clinical error is identified.

This is high-yield treatment knowledge, but currently a single-rule substitution with a named answer. The first-visit chronology appropriately precedes the later treatment-failure node, and its feedback does not name the later operation.
suggestions: Remove the key-specific 'had not tried' sentence and present prior therapy as a neutral treatment history.

Clarify that the requested plan targets fissure healing and use credible alternatives at the same treatment stage. Add a consequential patient-specific distinction only if supported, rather than labeling routine substitution hard.

title: Operative treatment of refractory high-pressure fissure

cues.phrase: Lateral internal sphincterotomy tailored to the fissure
cues.why: The key alone receives a reassuring patient-specific technical qualifier and is much longer than 'Anal fissurectomy' or 'Anocutaneous advancement flap'. It is the only visibly optimized operation.

fairness: Completed medical therapy, persistent fissure, elevated resting pressure and intact continence support LIS. Interpreting treatment failure and balancing pressure against continence risk are two consequential steps.
The flap and fissurectomy are relevant neighboring procedures. The explanation appropriately acknowledges continence risk; no confident clinical error is identified.

The later visit follows coherently from the nitrate-intolerance node and restates the necessary treatment history and functional observations. Prior feedback does not disclose LIS. This is a high-yield management decision.
suggestions: Use similarly specific procedure labels. Move the tailoring detail to feedback unless the actual scored comparison is extent of sphincter division; do not append filler qualifiers to the distractors.
Preserve the pressure, continence and prior-treatment findings that make the operative ranking fair.

title: Local evaluation after adequate negative colonoscopy

cues.phrase: Repeat complete colonoscopy
cues.why: The stem has already emphasized adequate preparation, cecal intubation and no colonic lesion during the same episode. This choice advertises repeating completed work.

cues.phrase: Endoanal ultrasound of the sphincter complex
cues.why: There is no continence or sphincter-injury problem. Compared with an anal-canal examination for bleeding and protrusion, the label is a conspicuously unrelated target.

fairness: Anoscopy is a reasonable remaining evaluation and the documented colonoscopy adequacy prevents an important ambiguity. Those necessary facts should not simply be deleted.

The alternatives do not test a credible competing inference. Selecting the only unperformed, relevant local examination is easy, despite the useful high-yield principle that colonoscopy does not replace targeted anorectal assessment.
The retrospective first-visit frame is clear. The explanation does not reveal the next node's banding answer. No confident clinical error is identified.
suggestions: Retain the quality of the previous assessment but compare plausible evaluations for a genuinely unresolved local finding, or request explicit acceptance as a foundational examination-sequence item.
Do not inflate difficulty through additional normal laboratory values or repeat-test foils.

title: Procedure selection after conservative treatment of internal hemorrhoids
fairness: Spontaneous reduction, no substantial external disease and persistent bleeding despite conservative care favor office rubber-band ligation over the supplied operative alternatives.

The resident must interpret prolapse behavior and combine it with disease extent and treatment stage. Artery ligation and excision are real treatment alternatives; the key is not merely the only treatment offered.
The prior anoscopy explanation does not name this procedure. The update supplies enough information to solve the later node independently, and the subsequent complication is not disclosed here.

The options are comparable named procedures. 'Office' describes a real treatment setting and is not paired with an explicit stem permission that independently selects it. This is high-yield management content; no confident clinical error is identified.
suggestions: Retain the raw reduction behavior and conservative-treatment failure. The explanation could briefly distinguish the nearest alternative by its role at this treatment stage without suggesting it is never appropriate.

title: Urgent evaluation of fever, pain and retention after banding
clarityIssues: 'Pelvic CT followed by reassessment before examination' does not distinguish immediate imaging during urgent surgical assessment from a clinically meaningful delay in source control.
The update gives fever and rapid pain progression but no current hemodynamic trajectory or local examination findings to help adjudicate immediate EUA versus rapid imaging first.

cues.phrase: Urgent anorectal examination under anesthesia
cues.why: Only the key contains an urgency signal, whereas both alternatives end in reassessment. Worsening pain and fever allow a generic 'choose the urgent response' strategy.

fairness: Recognizing possible perineal sepsis rather than isolated urinary retention, then seeking urgent anorectal source assessment after antibiotics, is a high-yield two-step decision.

Uncertainty: urgent EUA is defensible, but the supplied text does not fully establish that rapidly obtained pelvic CT before EUA is inferior in every represented clinical state. This is a close-option sequencing concern, not a confident claim that the key is clinically wrong.

Bladder drainage may be necessary concurrent care, but ward reassessment alone does not address the suspected anorectal source. The sequence after banding is coherent and the node supplies the relevant procedure history.
suggestions: Have the clinician resolve the exact imaging-versus-EUA ranking using supported patient findings and timing. Do not invent a universal time threshold or imply imaging must always precede or always be omitted.
Make urgency and supportive care comparable across options; compare the remaining source-assessment decisions rather than an urgent key against passive waiting.

title: Excision for persistent combined internal and external hemorrhoidal disease
fairness: Manual reduction, significant symptomatic external components and persistence after prior banding support excisional hemorrhoidectomy among the three named procedures.

The resident must interpret both prolapse severity and the symptom-generating external component, then recognize which intervention addresses that extent of disease after failed office care. The other procedures are plausible neighboring treatments rather than nonsurgical nonanswers.

There is no strong key-only lexical shortcut, diagnosis disclosure in a diagnosis task, or option-length cue. The first treatment node is coherent and high yield; no confident clinical inaccuracy is identified.

The later bleeding node raises a separate chronology concern about the absent complete colonic evaluation. Passing this procedure-selection text does not endorse deferring appropriate bleeding assessment until after surgery.
suggestions: The clause 'rather than a circumferential full-thickness cylinder' can be trimmed: no offered operation is for full-thickness rectal prolapse and the positive cushion findings already establish the represented anatomy.
Preserve the meaningful external symptoms and treatment history. Coordinate the separate bleeding-workup chronology when revising the companion node.

title: Persistent bleeding and iron deficiency after local healing
clarityIssues: The sequence establishes that a 55-year-old with bleeding underwent hemorrhoid treatment yet has never had complete colonic evaluation. It does not explain whether the earlier bleeding assessment was appropriately completed or whether the anemia and changed bleeding pattern are new.

cues.phrase: She had never had complete colonic evaluation.
cues.why: The named omission almost repeats 'Complete colonoscopy' and tells the learner exactly which task remains undone.

cues.phrase: anoscopy showed no bleeding lesion
cues.why: The first distractor repeats the completed local test after another wait despite continuing bleeding and iron deficiency. The second examines the healed surgical bed, leaving only one credible broader investigation.

fairness: Complete colonoscopy is a defensible best answer for continuing bleeding and iron-deficiency findings without prior complete colonic assessment. The explanation correctly resists attributing all bleeding to hemorrhoids.
The observation-to-action chain is currently too explicit to require two consequential inferences. This remains a high-yield safety principle, not a hard resident item.

The current update stands alone, and prior feedback does not name colonoscopy. The earlier-care chronology needs clarification so the teaching case does not appear to endorse a delayed initial bleeding workup. No exact earlier testing requirement is asserted from an offline review.
suggestions: Clarify the timing of anemia, bleeding-pattern change and previous evaluation. Keep the facts required for a single key without using a sentence that directly names the missing keyed action.
Compare credible next investigations for the actual residual question or seek explicit acceptance as a basic safety item; do not use two irrelevant local studies to manufacture difficulty.

title: Treating loose-stool urgency despite an old sphincter defect

cues.phrase: Pelvic-floor biofeedback for evacuation training
cues.why: The qualifier makes the competing therapy address evacuation rather than continence, while the stem explicitly supplies normal relaxation and an empty vault. This is an artificially mismatched form of a potentially relevant treatment.

cues.phrase: Loperamide with stool-consistency review
cues.why: Only this label directly targets the repeatedly emphasized loose-stool problem; both alternatives are framed around evacuation. The wording reinforces an already weak competitor set.

fairness: A monitored loperamide trial is reasonable for chronic loose-stool urgency after poorly tolerated bulking, with no represented inflammatory or infectious cause. No confident clinical error is identified.
The old defect could create a useful competing inference, but none of the options actually responds to it. The normal evacuation observations instead eliminate constipation-oriented choices.
The standalone case is coherent and the treatment principle is high yield. The current set permits a single symptom-to-drug match rather than two consequential decisions.
suggestions: Compare credible continence treatments at the same stage, rather than loperamide against two evacuation treatments. Keep treatment history sufficient to rank them.

Use the preserved ability to retain formed stool to make the old structural defect meaningfully compete with a reversible stool-related contributor. Do not portray all pelvic-floor rehabilitation as evacuation training.

title: Anatomical assessment after recurrent incontinence following repair
clarityIssues: 'Current procedural assessment' is broad. The need for present muscle anatomy is plausible when reconstruction is being considered, but the task should not imply that every procedural continence pathway requires ultrasound.

cues.phrase: current muscle continuity is undocumented
cues.why: This explicitly names the missing anatomical information rather than requiring its clinical relevance to be inferred.

cues.phrase: Repeat anorectal manometry with sensory testing
cues.why: Manometry has just supplied the physiological findings, so a repeat is a weak foil without a specific inadequacy. Defecography has no represented evacuation question, leaving ultrasound as the conspicuous remaining test.

fairness: Endoanal ultrasound can define present sphincter continuity and is a reasonable answer among these choices. Low pressures do not establish the anatomical defect. No confident clinical error is identified.
Distinguishing function from structure is high yield, but the named omission and completed-test foil reduce this to straightforward modality recall.
The case proceeds coherently to later procedural selection, but the explanation's caution about not reconstructing every defect partly previews that later comparison.
suggestions: Present the available old operative record and current findings without a sentence explicitly announcing the missing keyed datum; make the practical decision requiring anatomical clarification concrete.
Replace the redundant repeat-test foil with a credible competing assessment and reserve commentary on whether to reconstruct the defect for the later management answer.

title: Procedural choice after late failure of sphincter repair

cues.phrase: without implying that every defect should be reconstructed
cues.why: This preceding explanation directly warns against the next node's tempting repeat-reconstruction option before the learner sees the new ultrasound result. The phrase is a sequence cue, not leakage from the current node's own post-answer explanation.

fairness: Late deterioration after an initially effective repair, without a new injury and despite conservative treatment, makes a sacral neuromodulation trial a defensible best answer over repeating reconstruction or injecting a bulking agent.

Interpreting late functional failure despite an anatomical gap and using that course to choose a different therapeutic pathway are two consequential steps. The alternatives are named procedures of comparable scope, and the update is sufficiently self-contained.
This is high-yield continence management. No confident clinical error is identified; the principal revision is to preceding feedback so the exact sequence tests the intended reasoning.
suggestions: End the preceding explanation after the distinction between physiological dysfunction and anatomical mapping. Let the later deterioration and absence of new injury determine the repair-versus-neuromodulation choice here.
In this node's feedback, explicitly address why a residual defect does not by itself favor repeat repair and why the trial precedes permanent implantation.

title: Initial management of liquid seepage around rectal impaction
clarityIssues: 'Clear the retained stool and begin an evacuation regimen' does not name the actual proposed disimpaction action or maintenance treatment. It is less concrete than the named drug and rehabilitation alternatives.

cues.phrase: hard stool filling the vault with liquid at its edge
cues.why: The key 'Clear the retained stool' mirrors the explicitly described physical obstacle. The alternatives suppress stool frequency or defer to training, allowing a simple remove-the-obstacle shortcut.

fairness: The observations support overflow around retained rectal stool and favor clearance rather than loperamide. The absence of severe obstructive symptoms is useful safety context, not a cue to remove.

This is a high-yield recognition and safety item, but the mechanism is almost narrated and no credible competing immediate bowel plan remains. It does not meet the requested two-consequential-step difficulty.
Standalone chronology is clear and no confident clinical inaccuracy is identified in the general plan. Exact clearance and maintenance methods cannot be assessed because they are unnamed.
suggestions: Name a supported clearance method and subsequent bowel treatment, without inventing doses or timing.

Either seek explicit acceptance as a basic safety item or compare credible immediate bowel plans whose ranking depends on meaningful examination findings. Do not hide impaction or safety findings to make recognition harder.

title: Investigation of an intermittent evacuation-related bulge

cues.phrase: Fluoroscopic defecography during evacuation
cues.why: Only the key includes the activity repeatedly named in the presentation. The alternatives are a recently completed luminal examination and sphincter imaging, so activity-label matching selects the key.

cues.phrase: Recent colonoscopy found no luminal lesion.
cues.why: This explicitly weakens 'Repeat complete colonoscopy' without a changed indication or acquisition concern.

fairness: An intermittent bulge not reproduced during seated office straining, with possible multicompartment symptoms, reasonably warrants dynamic evacuation assessment. The key is defensible and no confident clinical error is identified.
The testability is high: residents should distinguish dynamic support problems from luminal disease. However, the current competitors do not require two consequential inferences.
The first-visit timeline and subsequent operative consultation are coherent. The explanation does not disclose a specific later operation.
suggestions: Compare credible investigations for the remaining mechanical question, or explicitly accept the node as foundational imaging selection.
Retain the failed provoked office examination and relevant compartment symptoms. Do not use repetition of a completed colonoscopy as the principal distractor.

title: Operation for long full-thickness prolapse with anesthetic constraints
fairness: The long full-thickness segment and documented limitation on general anesthesia and pneumoperitoneum support perineal rectosigmoidectomy among the supplied operations. Delorme remains a credible perineal alternative whose suitability depends on the represented extent.

The anesthetic constraint rules against the laparoscopic route but does not select between the two perineal operations. It is decision-critical information rather than a key-only availability permission. Combining operative risk with prolapse extent supplies two consequential steps.

The 12 cm value is a patient observation, not a universal threshold established by this review. Exact comparative surgical ranking remains for clinician sign-off; no confident error is identified from the visible text.
The later node restates the prolapse anatomy, viability and anesthesia assessment and follows coherently from diagnostic evaluation. This is high-yield operative selection, not hard-level reasoning.
suggestions: Keep both perineal alternatives and the documented anesthesia assessment. Explain the relative suitability of the long segment without converting its length into an unsupported absolute cutoff.

title: Treating impaired evacuation coordination despite a structural pouch
fairness: Anal pressure rising during attempted evacuation together with abnormal balloon expulsion supports impaired coordination. Persistent symptoms despite soft stool and a coexisting pouch make biofeedback before structural surgery a defensible next step.

The resident must interpret concordant functional results, then prioritize the functional contributor over the tempting structural finding. Rectocele repair and puborectalis injection are clinically related alternatives, not different-category foils.

The keyed label describes the treatment without giving a pre-answer rationale. Its greater length is not enough to establish a useful nonmedical shortcut in this set. The objective is high yield and no confident clinical error is identified.

This first node is coherent. Its explanation is appropriate for this answer, but the same explanation and the early repair option scaffold the eventual repair node; that sequence limitation is recorded there.
suggestions: Preserve the concordant raw physiological observations and the distinction between an anatomical pouch and proof that it causes retained stool. Do not replace them with the diagnostic label before the choice.
When revising the later repair node, ensure it tests a distinct remaining decision rather than simply completing the sequence announced here.

title: Dynamic assessment after improved evacuation coordination
clarityIssues: The explanation's sentence about 'a repeat justified by an omitted report sentence' discusses an authoring repair, not the patient's clinical reasoning. It is distracting in learner-facing feedback.

cues.phrase: without rectal contrast or an evacuation phase
cues.why: The key is 'Defecography with recorded contrast evacuation'. The explicit missing components almost assemble the answer label.

cues.phrase: Repeat anorectal manometry and balloon expulsion
cues.why: The stem has just documented improvement on both tests. The other distractor evaluates sphincters without a stated continence problem, leaving only the new dynamic investigation credible.

fairness: Dynamic assessment of persistent splinting after functional improvement is reasonable. The actual acquisition record, rather than an omitted report phrase, appropriately establishes that the previous study was static; this necessary distinction must survive revision.

The case follows coherently from biofeedback and provides enough current context to stand alone. Nevertheless, the answer follows from the conspicuous acquisition omission even without interpreting the functional response, so two consequential steps are not established.
This is high-yield diagnostic reasoning in principle. No confident clinical error is identified in obtaining defecography.
suggestions: Retain truthful acquisition details, but change the decision or competitor set so the response trajectory and residual symptom mechanism are necessary to choose among credible plans.
Remove the authoring-process sentence from learner feedback and avoid previewing exactly which future result will trigger the next node's operation.

title: Repair discussion for retained rectocele contents after functional treatment
clarityIssues: 'Repeat evacuation imaging' conflicts with the preceding record: the earlier MRI was static, and the immediately preceding node requested the first recorded contrast evacuation acquisition. Identify the newly returned study without suggesting an unexplained second dynamic test.

For standalone use, 'Coordination and balloon expulsion remain improved' does not explicitly restate that biofeedback was completed and functional testing now normalized. That treatment boundary matters to the remaining injection option.

cues.phrase: Biofeedback addresses that contributor before deciding whether the coexisting rectocele requires repair.
cues.why: The first node's explanation previews this eventual repair decision, and 'Native-tissue rectocele repair' has already appeared as an earlier option.

cues.phrase: a contrast evacuation study can establish whether the pouch retains material and changes treatment
cues.why: The immediately preceding explanation predicts the exact finding now supplied. The sequence partly rehearses the finding-to-action inference rather than leaving both steps independent.

fairness: Persistent disabling evacuation symptoms, contrast retained in the pouch and release with vaginal pressure support a causal structural contributor after functional treatment. These observations can sustain two consequential steps in isolation.

Native-tissue repair is a defensible preferred pathway, but the explanation only justifies discussing repair in general. It does not explain the comparative disadvantage of stapled transanal rectal resection, the closest structural-procedure alternative. Exact contemporary procedural ranking was not source-verified in this offline review; no categorical clinical error is asserted.

The general objective is high yield. Sequence scaffolding, the imaging chronology and the underexplained close alternative prevent passing this exact version as an independently reasoned later decision.
suggestions: Call this the returned evacuation study, explicitly state the completed functional treatment and current objective response, and preserve the splinting-linked retention that makes the structural finding consequential.
Revise earlier feedback so it does not predict this exact result-to-repair pathway. Alternatively make this node test a distinct remaining supported surgical decision.

Have the clinician verify the close procedural ranking and add concise feedback explaining why the stapled alternative is less appropriate here; do not invent a numerical size threshold or universal route ranking.
